To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prior exposure to repeated stress exacerbates the splenic inflammatory response induced by lipopolisaccharide, which may be due to changes in catecholamines and adrenergic receptors.
repeated stress exacerbates lipopolysaccha-ride-induced inflammatory response in the spleens of rats by altering catecholamines and adrenergic receptors.
repeated immobilization stress exacerbates LPS-induced inflammatory response in the spleens of rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the stress system in the regulation of the immune response in the rat spleen.
the mechanisms by which prior stress influences the innate immune functions in the spleen.
the role of catecholamine-mediated sympathetic innervation in the regulation of splenic immunity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
repeated stress exaggerates the inflammatory immune response in the rat spleen.

prior stress exposure, in this case immobilization stress, may exacerbate the immune response to a subsequent immunogenic stimulus, such as LPS, by increasing the recruitment of peripheral immune cells to the spleen.

repeated stress exaggerates the inflammatory reaction in the spleen, which is mediated by the changes in catecholamine levels and specific adrenoceptor subtypes, resulting in increased infiltration of monocytes and induction of apoptosis within the spleen.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
repeated stress exposure via sympathetic activation exaggerates the innate immune response to LPS in the spleen.
the repeated stress exacerbates LPS-induced inflammatory response in the spleens via changes in catecholamine levels and adrenergic receptors.

repeated stress via specific α- and β-AR subtypes exacerbates the inflammatory response in the spleens of rats, and the mechanisms of this effect may be associated with the recruitment of peripheral monocytes and neutrophils to this organ, resulting in the induction of apoptosis in B cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prior stress history may modulate immune response induced by an immunogen, which could be important in the development of stress-associated diseases.

repeated stress may exacerbate the inflammatory response in the spleens of rats, likely by increasing the number of circulating monocytes and neutrolphils and inducing apoptosis within the splenic tissue, particularly in the B cell population.
prior stress exposure may modulate the innate immune response and thus may affect the course of the disease.
